common_name: Rugel's Yellow Pitcher Plant (Maroon-Throated Sarracenia Flava Variety)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into a wet, acidic peat-and-sand bog mix in full sun, and keep the pot standing in pure rain or distilled water year-round; rugelii tends to throw the tallest, most robust pitchers of the seven recognized flava color forms, so give it extra room compared with typical yellow pitcher plant.

directions: Rugelii is a naturally occurring color form of the yellow pitcher plant marked by a distinctive dark maroon patch spreading across the throat and inner mouth of an otherwise clear yellow-green pitcher, a pattern absent from plain-colored flava. It ranks among the largest-pitchered of the flava variants and is concentrated in peninsular Florida and southern Georgia bogs, making it well suited to warm Gulf Coast garden conditions. Grow it exactly as the species: permanently saturated, nutrient-poor peat-sand medium, full sun, and irrigation with only rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, since minerals and fertilizer damage the fine root system. Divide congested rhizome clumps in early spring to maintain vigorous pitcher production.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)
Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

common_name: Ornate Yellow Pitcher Plant (Net-Veined Sarracenia Flava Variety)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into a wet, acidic peat-and-sand bog mix in full sun, keeping the pot standing in pure rain or distilled water year-round; ornata shows its intricate red network best on pitchers that develop in strong, unfiltered sun.

directions: Ornata is distinguished from other flava color forms by a fine, dense network of red veining that covers almost the entire pitcher tube and hood rather than being confined to the throat, giving the trap a lace-like, heavily patterned look, along with a red throat patch at the mouth. This variety occurs scattered through the wider flava range across the Atlantic and Gulf Coastal Plain and often intergrades with rugelii and cuprea forms where populations meet. Maintain it in a permanently wet, nutrient-poor bog medium of peat and sand, watering only with rain or distilled water, and provide full sun so the netted red patterning develops fully. Divide crowded clumps in early spring once new growth begins.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

common_name: Copper Top Pitcher Plant (Bronze-Hooded Sarracenia Flava Variety)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions in spring into a wet, acidic peat-and-sand bog mix in full sun, keeping the pot standing in pure rain or distilled water year-round; the coppery hood color of cuprea intensifies with strong, direct sun exposure and fades in shade.

directions: Copper top pitcher plant carries an arching hood and upper pitcher wall flushed in bronze to coppery-orange, contrasting sharply against the lime-green to yellow lower tube, a color combination unique among the flava varieties. It occurs naturally as a scattered form within Atlantic Coastal Plain populations, most notably in the Carolinas, rather than forming its own separate range. Grow it in a permanently saturated, nutrient-poor peat-sand medium in full sun, since strong light exposure is what produces the richest copper tone in the hood. Water only with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water and divide congested rhizomes in early spring to keep the clump vigorous.

common_name: All-Green Purple Pitcher Plant (Heterophylla Pigment-Free Variety)

planting.note: Set transplants into a 1:1 mix of peat moss and perlite or pure long-fiber sphagnum moss in partial shade, never fertilized potting mix or garden soil, and keep the pot sitting in a tray of rain or distilled water at all times; give this pigment-free form a distinct cold winter dormancy like the typical species.

directions: This naturally occurring mutant form of the purple pitcher plant has lost the ability to produce red anthocyanin pigment, so its squat, deeply cupped pitchers stay a luminous, electric green even under bright sun where typical purpurea would flush deep maroon-red. The nodding flowers likewise open pale yellow-green rather than the wine-red of the pigmented species, and scattered plants of this heterophylla form turn up within otherwise normally colored purpurea bog populations from the Great Lakes region into eastern Canada. Grow it exactly as the species, in a permanently wet, nutrient-poor medium of pure sphagnum or a peat-perlite blend, watering only with rain or distilled water and never applying fertilizer or standard potting soil. It needs a true cold winter rest with reduced light and moisture to flower and pitcher reliably the following season.

common_name: Okefenokee Giant Pitcher Plant (Sarracenia Minor Var. Okefenokeensis)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown transplants in spring in wet to saturated, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum in full sun to partial shade; this giant form needs a deeper pot or bog bed than typical hooded pitcher plant to accommodate its much taller pitchers.

directions: This robust regional form of the hooded pitcher plant is confined to the Okefenokee Swamp of southern Georgia and adjacent northern Florida, where it produces dramatically taller, more upright pitchers than typical Sarracenia minor, sometimes reaching close to three feet compared with the two feet or less common in the wider species range. Its domed hood still arches tightly over the mouth and the upper tube still carries rows of translucent white windows that disorient trapped insects, but the overall proportions are noticeably more massive and woody-looking. Grow it as you would typical hooded pitcher plant, in a permanently wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peat or sphagnum medium watered only with rain or distilled water, in full sun to light shade. Give it a wider pot or deeper bog bed than the species to support its taller growth, and divide the spreading rhizome clump every few years in spring.
sources: Carnivorous Plants of the Southeast (Larry Mellichamp)

common_name: Juthatip Soper Pitcher Plant (Hot Pink-and-White Sarracenia Hybrid)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in spring and set into pure long-fiber sphagnum moss or a 1:1 peat-perlite mix, keeping the pot standing in rain or distilled water at all times; this registered hybrid holds its saturated pink-and-white pitcher color best in full, unfiltered sun.

directions: Bred in the United Kingdom from a cross of Sarracenia leucophylla and Sarracenia purpurea, this ICPS-registered cultivar produces broad, upright pitchers mottled and veined in vivid hot pink, white, and red, a bolder and more saturated color combination than either parent species shows alone. The intensity of the pink coloring increases through the growing season and is strongest on pitchers that mature in full, direct sun. Grow it exactly as any garden Sarracenia: a permanently saturated, nutrient-poor peat-sand or sphagnum bog medium, irrigation with only rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water, and a reduced-light, reduced-water winter rest. Divide the clumping rhizome every few years in early spring as new growth resumes.
sources: International Carnivorous Plant Society (ICPS Cultivar Registry)

common_name: Snowdrift Mountain Laurel (Compact Pure White-Flowered Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; avoid soggy sites and heavy afternoon sun. Snowdrift stays compact and rounded, so it needs less room than large species-type mountain laurel.

directions: Snowdrift opens clean, pure white buds and flowers without the pink flush or banding seen in most mountain laurel cultivars, giving it a bright, luminous presence against dark evergreen foliage in the late spring border. It forms a tidy, dense, rounded shrub noticeably more compact than the wild species, making it easier to fit into a smaller shade garden or foundation planting. Site in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled or part shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to conserve moisture and maintain soil acidity. As with all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Raspberry Glow Mountain Laurel (Burgundy Bud to Raspberry-Pink Flower Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil, siting in part shade for the best flower color retention; Raspberry Glow is a sibling selection of the cultivar Sarah from the same Connecticut breeding program.

directions: Raspberry Glow opens deep burgundy-red buds that expand into flowers of a bright raspberry-pink brushed with white toward the petal edges, a richer, more saturated pink than most banded mountain laurel cultivars offer. It was raised by the same Connecticut breeding program responsible for the red-budded cultivar Sarah, and shares its compact, sturdy, well-branched habit. Grow in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in part shade, protecting it from harsh afternoon sun which can bleach the flower color and scorch foliage. Like all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.

common_name: Pristine Mountain Laurel (Heat-Tolerant Pure White Selection)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Pristine was selected in South Carolina and tolerates heat and humidity better than many northern mountain laurel cultivars, making it a strong choice for Deep South gardens.

directions: Pristine was discovered as a chance seedling in Aiken County, South Carolina, and stands out for opening flawless, brilliant white flowers with almost no pink blush, a purer white than most mountain laurel selections show. Because it originated in the hot, humid Deep South rather than the cooler Appalachian range typical of the species, it handles southern summer heat unusually well for a mountain laurel. Site in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, mulching with pine bark or pine straw to keep roots cool and moist through summer heat. As with all mountain laurel, every part of the plant is toxic if ingested.
